title: Recommendation Engine
seoTitle: Design a Recommendation System Like Netflix's
description: Design a recommendation engine — candidate generation, ranking, feature stores, offline training vs. online serving, and feedback loops.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a Recommendation Engine?
blocks.text: A recommendation engine picks which items — movies, products, videos — to show each user, ordered by how likely they are to engage. Netflix's home rows and Amazon's "customers also bought" are classic examples.

items: Users should see a personalised list of recommended items on the home page.
Recommendations should adapt to user behaviour (views, ratings, purchases).

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Scale to 200M users and millions of items.
Fresh enough: new behaviour reflected within minutes to hours; new items recommendable within a day.
Highly available — fall back to popular items rather than show nothing.
**Interaction**: user × item events (view, click, rating, purchase) with timestamps.
**Embedding**: learned vector representing a user or item.
**Feature**: precomputed signals used for ranking (e.g. user's genre affinity, item popularity).

blocks.code:
GET /recommendations?userId&context=home&limit=50 -> Item[]
GET /items/:id/similar?limit=20 -> Item[]
POST /events { userId, itemId, type, ts }   (behaviour logging)

items: **Candidate generation** cheaply pulls ~1,000 plausible items from several sources: nearest neighbours of the user's embedding in a vector index, items similar to recently watched ones, and trending items.

**Ranking** scores the candidates with a richer model using features from a **feature store** (user history, item stats, context like time of day) and returns the top results, with business rules (remove already-watched, diversify genres).

blocks.text: Precompute each item's nearest neighbours offline (by embedding similarity or co-occurrence: "people who watched X also watched Y") and store the lists in a key-value store for instant lookup.

Interaction events stream through Kafka. Offline pipelines retrain models and recompute embeddings daily; a streaming job updates real-time features (e.g. "last 5 items watched") so the ranker reacts within minutes.
1) How do we serve within 200ms for 200M users?

blocks.title: Score every item at request time

approach.text: Run the ranking model over the whole catalog.

challenges.text: Millions of model evaluations per request is far too slow.

approach.text: A nightly batch job computes each user's top 100 and stores them; serving is a key lookup.

challenges.text: Fast, but stale — it ignores what the user did five minutes ago, and wastes work on inactive users.

blocks.title: Online two-stage funnel with precomputed embeddings

approach.text: Precompute embeddings offline, use approximate nearest-neighbour search (e.g. HNSW) for candidates in milliseconds, then rank a few hundred items online with fresh features. Cache results per user for a short time and fall back to precomputed or popular lists on timeouts.

challenges.text: More infrastructure: vector index, feature store and model serving must all meet latency budgets.

blocks.text: 2) How do we handle new users and new items?

The **cold-start** problem: new users have no history, and new items have no interactions. For users, start from popular and trending items, onboarding preferences, and context (country, device). For items, use content features (genre, description embeddings) to place them near similar items, and reserve a small amount of exposure to gather signal (exploration).
3) How do we avoid training/serving skew?

Compute features in one place — a **feature store** with the same definitions for offline training and online serving — and log the exact features used at serving time so training data matches production.

quiz.question: Why split recommendation serving into candidate generation and ranking?
options: Ranking the full catalog per request is too slow; cheap retrieval narrows candidates first
quiz.explanation: A funnel keeps expensive models on a small set.

quiz.question: What does approximate nearest-neighbour search provide?
options: Fast retrieval of items with embeddings close to the user's
quiz.explanation: ANN indexes like HNSW find similar vectors in milliseconds.

quiz.question: How do you recommend to a brand-new user?
options: Popular/trending items, onboarding choices and context
quiz.explanation: Cold-start relies on non-personal signals until history accrues.

quiz.question: What is a feature store for?
options: Consistent feature definitions for both training and serving
